title: Cranial Nerve I (The Olfactory Nerve)
subtitle: Where a smell deficit places the lesion: nasal disease, nerve filaments, bulb/tract, or frontal-temporal cortex

points.text: Olfactory filaments cross the cribriform plate of the ethmoid to reach the olfactory bulb, so a cribriform fracture can tear them.
points.quote: These bundles, the filaments of the olfactory nerve, penetrate the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone and enter the olfactory bulb.

points.text: In the bulb the afferent fibers synapse on the second-order neurons, the mitral and tufted cells.
points.quote: the olfactory afferent fibers synapse with the dendrites of the second-order neurons called the mitral and tufted cells

points.text: The tract runs back in the olfactory sulcus on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe, which is why frontal masses can reach it.
points.quote: The axons of the mitral and tufted cells leave the olfactory bulb and course posteriorly, as the olfactory tract, in the olfactory sulcus

points.text: Some strial fibers cross in the anterior commissure to the opposite hemisphere; others go to the ipsilateral piriform lobe.
points.quote: Some of these strial fibers decussate in the anterior commissure and join the fibers from the opposite olfactory pathways

points.text: The piriform cortex is the largest cortical olfactory area, at the frontal-temporal junction.
points.quote: The piriform cortex (area 51) is the largest cortical olfactory area

points.text: Test each nostril separately with nonirritating substances; perceiving a smell matters more than naming it.
points.quote: perception of the smell is of more value than identification of the specific substance

points.text: Avoid ammonia-type irritants, because they stimulate trigeminal fibers rather than purely testing CN I.
points.quote: Irritating substances (e.g., ammonia) are to be avoided because they stimulate the trigeminal nerve fibers in the nasal mucosa

localizationRules.explanation: Before localizing to the nervous system, look for local nasal disease or an upper respiratory infection, especially when the loss is bilateral.
localizationRules.quote: must first be sought as the cause of anosmia, especially if the olfactory difficulty is bilateral

localizationRules.rule: Unilateral anosmia points to the pre-decussation pathway
localizationRules.explanation: After nasal disease is excluded, unilateral anosmia suggests a lesion of the filaments, bulb, tract or stria.
localizationRules.quote: anosmia, especially unilateral anosmia, should raise the suspicion of a lesion affecting the olfactory nerve filaments, bulb, tract, or stria

localizationRules.rule: Distal to the decussation, no deficit
localizationRules.explanation: Cortical representation is bilateral, so a unilateral lesion beyond the crossing does not cause anosmia.
localizationRules.quote: a unilateral lesion distal to the decussation of the olfactory fibers causes no olfactory impairment

localizationRules.explanation: Frontal lobe masses may produce anosmia before obvious frontal signs, so test smell in any patient with personality change or subtle frontal signs.
localizationRules.quote: often exert pressure on the olfactory system and may lead to anosmia even before clear-cut frontal lobe signs

localizationRules.rule: Trauma disrupts fibers before the decussation
localizationRules.explanation: Head injury is a leading cause of anosmia through damage to the olfactory fibers, with or without a fracture.
localizationRules.quote: is probably the most common cause of disruption of the olfactory fibers before their decussation

keySyndromes.name: Foster-Kennedy syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral anosmia + ipsilateral optic atrophy + contralateral papilledema
keySyndromes.clue: Seen with olfactory groove or sphenoid ridge masses or frontal space-occupying lesions; the atrophy is on the side of the mass and the papilledema on the opposite side.
keySyndromes.quote: The Foster-Kennedy syndrome is occasionally noted with olfactory groove or sphenoid ridge masses (especially meningiomas) or space-occupying lesions of the frontal lobe.

keySyndromes.name: Pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Previous unilateral optic atrophy + raised intracranial pressure of any cause + papilledema only in the other eye
keySyndromes.clue: Unlike the true syndrome, no frontal mass is required; the atrophic disc cannot swell.
keySyndromes.quote: Because the atrophic disc cannot become swollen, only the previously normal fundus demonstrates papilledema.

keySyndromes.name: Esthesioneuroblastoma
keySyndromes.clue: Arises from olfactory neuroepithelium near the ethmoid sinus and may extend into the orbit.
keySyndromes.quote: These tumors may present with anosmia as well as persistent nasal obstruction and epistaxis

keySyndromes.name: Kallmann syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Permanent anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (+ possible cerebellar ataxia and mirror movements)
keySyndromes.clue: A familial syndrome combining a smell deficit with an endocrine deficit.
keySyndromes.quote: A familial syndrome of permanent anosmia with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann syndrome) has also been described

keySyndromes.name: Olfactory epileptic aura
keySyndromes.triad: Olfactory hallucination + partial seizure with complex symptomatology (+ amygdala as likely symptomatogenic zone)
keySyndromes.clue: The aura is not necessarily unpleasant; tumors are the commonest cause in this group.
keySyndromes.quote: In patients with olfactory epileptic auras, tumors are the most common etiology of the seizures, and mesial temporal sclerosis is relatively rare

boardTraps.text: The side of impact matters: frontal blows cause less olfactory dysfunction than occipital or lateral blows.
boardTraps.quote: Frontal impact produces less dysfunction than back (occipital) or side impacts

boardTraps.text: Anosmia does not require a fracture; closed head injury alone can disrupt the pathways on one or both sides.
boardTraps.quote: but closed head injury without fracture may also disrupt the olfactory pathways unilaterally or bilaterally

boardTraps.text: Many cases labelled Foster-Kennedy may in fact be due to compression of both optic nerves.
boardTraps.quote: Many cases of Foster-Kennedy syndrome may actually be due to direct bilateral optic nerve compression

boardTraps.text: A pseudo-Foster-Kennedy picture is most often sequential anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or optic neuritis.
boardTraps.quote: A pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome is most often due to sequential anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (arteritic or nonarteritic) or optic neuritis

boardTraps.text: Anosmia is expected in Parkinson disease; anosmia in suspected PSP or corticobasal degeneration is atypical and should prompt diagnostic review.
boardTraps.quote: Anosmia in suspected progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration is atypical and should likewise provoke diagnostic review.

boardTraps.text: Olfactory damage after anterior communicating aneurysm surgery depends on the approach.
boardTraps.quote: Olfactory damage is much more common after an anterior interhemispheric surgical approach rather than after a basal interhemispheric approach.
